summary: Describes a private SIP header for ETSI TISPAN to authorize early media flows in 3GPP IMS networks. It is useful in interconnected SIP networks that must control media before a call is answered. It is informational.

eli5.summary: A permission slip that says whether sounds can play before someone picks up.

subtitle: A SIP header to control who can send and receive sounds before a call is answered.

tldr.problem: When SIP networks with different early media policies interconnect, they cannot reliably control whether audio is transmitted before a call is answered, risking unauthorized user data exchange.
tldr.mechanism: The P-Early-Media header field (for use within trusted networks) lets a boundary SIP server signal to peers which parties are authorized to send or receive early media, using direction parameters like sendrecv, sendonly, recvonly, or inactive.
tldr.outcome: Networks that interconnect can now enforce compatible early media policies, enabling safe gateway handoff and preventing unwanted data exchange before call answer.

today: RFC 5009 is an Informational specification defining a private SIP header for early media authorization within trusted domains. It is used in 3GPP IMS networks and ETSI TISPAN deployments where early media control between interconnected networks is needed. The document remains current and has not been obsoleted or updated, though adoption remains limited to specialized closed-network deployments that meet the strict trust domain requirements.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
In traditional phone networks (PSTN), before a call is answered, the calling party hears ringing or announcements, and the called party can sometimes send touch-tone signals for special handling, like entering a credit card number. These early media flows do not involve direct data exchange between end users—only call signaling information.

In SIP (Session Initiation Protocol) networks, early media can technically carry any user data, not just call progress signals. Different networks may have different policies on whether to allow early media at all. When two SIP networks interconnect, they cannot easily know whether the other network's early media policy is compatible with theirs. For instance, Network A might allow early audio only from a PSTN gateway, while Network B allows it from any user equipment, creating a risk of unintended data exchange.

The P-Early-Media header provides a solution for networks that form a trust domain—a group of servers within a single administrative boundary that trust each other. Within such a domain, boundary servers can use this header to signal to peer servers whether early media is authorized, enabling networks with different policies to interconnect safely.
sections.eli5: SIP is the protocol for internet calls. Before you answer, the system might play sounds or let you send signals. This header tells everyone whether that is allowed.

sections.title: Early Media Types and Authorization
sections.content:
Backward early media flows from the called party (User Agent Server) to the calling party (User Agent Client). In PSTN networks, this includes ringing tones, announcements, and requests for further information (like digit collection). These flows carry no user data.

Forward early media flows from the calling party to the called party, used (in PSTN) for secondary dialing or responses. Again, it is directed at network servers, not other users.

In a SIP network with a PSTN gateway as the called party, early media is typically desirable because the gateway provides call progress information. When the called party is user equipment (a phone or computer), the network usually wants to gate off early media to prevent unauthorized data exchange.

When networks interconnect, a boundary server cannot know the policy of the peer network. The P-Early-Media header lets the server making early media decisions communicate its policy to others in the trust domain, ensuring coherent enforcement across the interconnected networks.
sections.eli5: Sounds coming back to the caller are backward early media. Signals the caller sends before the call is answered are forward. The header says what each side is allowed to do.

sections.title: The P-Early-Media Header Field
sections.content:
The P-Early-Media header contains direction parameters that specify early media authorization per media line in the session. The allowed values are:

  • sendrecv: early media in both directions (from called to calling and vice versa)
  • sendonly: early media only from called to calling (backward only)
  • recvonly: early media only from calling to called (forward only)
  • inactive: no early media authorized

A User Agent Client may include the header with the "supported" parameter in an INVITE request to signal that it recognizes the header. A User Agent Server (the called party) may insert the header in responses (like 180 Ringing or 183 Session Progress) to request early media authorization. Each proxy in the path can add, modify, or remove the header based on local policy and trust relationships.

If a proxy also implements media gating (actively blocking or allowing media flows), it uses the header parameters to decide which gates to open, and may add a "gated" parameter to signal that it is already enforcing the authorization.

The header does not interact with the SDP offer/answer process; early media authorization is independent of the SDP direction attributes. The most recent P-Early-Media header received applies until the 200 OK final response is sent, at which point all media is implicitly authorized.
sections.eli5: The header says sendrecv (both ways), sendonly (backward), recvonly (forward), or inactive (nothing). Each message can have its own permission.

sections.title: Procedures and Limitations
sections.content:
At the calling party (UAC), receiving a P-Early-Media header allows the caller to decide whether to gate or cut through early media, and whether to play received audio instead of generating local ringback.

At the called party (UAS), the header signals whether early media it wants to send is authorized. If the INVITE did not carry the header, the called party may suppress its own early media authorization requests.

At a proxy, if media gating is performed, the header parameters control which gates open. Boundary proxies enforce trust domain policy by removing headers from untrusted sources.

The header has limitations. It does not apply when early media uses the early-session content disposition type. When parallel forking occurs (sending the INVITE to multiple destinations), the calling party cannot reliably correlate which authorization applies to which forked dialog unless symmetric RTP is used. The RFC recommends using the most restrictive authorization received and disabling parallel forking if early media is required.

Media gating interacts with NAT traversal and tunneling protocols in ways that must be carefully designed to avoid media clipping or loss.
sections.eli5: The server that plays sounds can ask for permission. The server that receives sounds can check the permission. When calls split (parallel forking), it is harder to track which permission applies where.

sections.title: Trust Domain and Security
sections.content:
This extension is only for use within a trust domain, defined in RFC 3325 as a group of servers under a single administrative boundary where all users and servers explicitly trust each other to enforce policy correctly.

The P-Early-Media header is not suitable for general internet use. It lacks cryptographic certification of the direction parameters, making it vulnerable to forgery, replay, and falsification if used outside a trust domain. The header does not identify who is making the request, so the trust domain must assume it is made by a trusted member.

Within a trust domain, integrity of the header parameters across hops between servers is important. Boundary servers must police the header at network edges, removing it from untrusted external sources and verifying that internal headers have not been forged by external peers. Pair-wise security associations (like TLS) between servers in the trust domain help verify the source.

Attacks such as spoofing early media or impersonating a trusted server are outside the scope of this mechanism's defenses.
sections.eli5: This only works when all the servers trust each other. On the open Internet, bad actors could forge these messages, so it is not safe there.
